diagrams.name: mat-p421-base-liner
diagrams.title: Base and liner under a restoration

cloze.text: Bases {{c1::insulate}} and protect the tooth and act as a {{c2::substitute for the dentin}} removed during caries preparation.
Bases provide {{c1::thermal and chemical}} protection and can also resist {{c2::condensation}} forces.
Liners {{c1::seal dentinal tubules}} and protect against leakage of irritants present in the saliva and restorative materials.
Unlike bases, liners cannot resist {{c1::compressive}} forces.
Zinc oxide-eugenol (ZOE) combines zinc oxide powder with {{c1::eugenol}} liquid, also called {{c2::oil of cloves}}.
ZOE is dispensed as {{c1::two separate pastes}}.
ZOE can irritate tissues, and some patients are {{c1::allergic to oil of cloves}}.
ZOE is used as a liner for its {{c1::obtundent (sedative)}} effect on the pulp, especially useful when deep cavity preparations may lead to post-treatment sensitivity.
ZOE is also used as an {{c1::impression material}} during construction of {{c2::complete dentures}}.
ZOE is used as a {{c1::temporary filling (intermediate restorative material)}} for a few days before placement of the final filling.
The consistency of ZOE is described as {{c1::putty-like}}.
ZOE provides {{c1::anesthetic}} and {{c2::antibacterial}} properties.
ZOE {{c1::interferes with polymerization}} of composites — it prevents resin from setting.
cloze.extra: So never place ZOE under a composite or resin cement.

cloze.text: {{c1::Zinc phosphate}} is one of the oldest and most widely used cements — around since the 1800s.
cloze.extra: Did you know: it was the go-to for crowns and bridges for over a century, even though it doesn't bond to teeth and can sting the pulp.

cloze.text: Zinc phosphate cement = zinc oxide powder + {{c1::phosphoric acid}} liquid.
Mixing zinc phosphate causes an {{c1::exothermic}} reaction, so a cool {{c2::glass slab}} is used to dissipate the heat.
Zinc phosphate is bonded to the tooth through {{c1::mechanical interlocking}} (it does not bond chemically).
Polycarboxylate cement is mainly used for permanent cementation of {{c1::orthodontic bands and brackets}}.
Polycarboxylate powder is primarily {{c1::zinc oxide}}, with smaller amounts of {{c2::magnesium oxide}} and {{c3::stannous fluoride}}.
Polycarboxylate liquid is a thick {{c1::polyacrylic acid copolymer}} in water.
For luting, polycarboxylate should {{c1::adhere to the spatula when raised an inch}}; as a base it should be {{c2::stickier}}.
Polycarboxylate must be applied before it develops a {{c1::dull and/or sinewy}} appearance.
Polycarboxylate is useful under composites because it {{c1::does not interfere with polymerization}}, and its setting reaction does not {{c2::release heat}}.
Glass ionomer cement binds to {{c1::dentin}} and releases {{c2::fluoride}}.
Glass ionomer is commonly used in {{c1::Class V}} restorations because of its fluoride-releasing ability.
Glass ionomer's {{c1::coefficient of thermal expansion}} is similar to that of the natural tooth.
For luting orthodontic work, glass ionomer should be {{c1::creamy and glossy}}; as a base, it should be {{c2::stickier}}.
Resin cements are mostly {{c1::BIS-GMA (bisphenol A-glycidyl methacrylate)}} and other dimethacrylate monomers; the filler is {{c2::silica}}.
Resin is commonly used as a {{c1::cement}} to retain restorations.
Before a resin cement, an {{c1::etchant or silane coupling agent}} must be applied to the tooth to achieve mechanical or chemical bonding.
Besides cements, resins are used in dental {{c1::sealants}} and fluoride {{c2::varnishes}}.
Calcium hydroxide is used as a liner or base, and also as a {{c1::root canal filling material}}.
Calcium hydroxide (Dycal) is a {{c1::two-paste}} system dispensed at {{c2::equal lengths}}.
Calcium hydroxide can stimulate the production of {{c1::reparative dentin}}.
Cavity varnish is a liner applied under {{c1::gold/amalgam}} restorations.
Cavity varnish numbs pain, blocks penetration of chemicals, and {{c1::seals dentinal tubules}} to prevent transfer of {{c2::heat/cold}}.
Conditioning (etching) removes the {{c1::smear layer}} and creates {{c2::microscopic pores}} that allow resin materials to flow in and bond mechanically.
Etching time: enamel {{c1::15–30}} seconds; dentin {{c2::10–15}} seconds.
Primary teeth often require {{c1::longer}} etching times (up to {{c2::30–60}} seconds) due to their more mineralized outer enamel layer.
Finishing removes excess material and produces {{c1::smooth}} surfaces, which decrease {{c2::plaque accumulation}} and tissue irritation.
{{c1::Margination (recontouring)}} removes excess restorative material with knives, files, strips, finishing burs, stones, discs, etc.
{{c1::Ultrasonic scalers}} are best for removing overhangs.
Margination does NOT correct an {{c1::open margin}}.
Polishing follows finishing and creates a smooth, {{c1::glossy}} finish that decreases plaque accumulation.
{{c1::Tarnish}} is discoloration due to {{c2::oxidation}} of the surface material; polishing can remove it and reproduce a smooth surface.
{{c1::Amalgams}} are susceptible to tarnishing; {{c2::gold}} is not.
Use {{c1::selective polishing}} to preserve tooth structure when possible.
cloze.extra: Board Alert: if you see the words "selective polishing", that is always the answer.

cloze.text: {{c1::Larger, harder}} grits are more abrasive; more {{c2::pressure}} and more {{c3::speed}} are also more abrasive and create heat.
Use {{c1::lubrication}} when polishing to prevent overheating.
Total enamel thickness is about {{c1::2,000–2,500}} microns.
cloze.extra: Medium-grit paste removes up to 4 microns in 30 s — small, but it adds up with repeated polishing.

cloze.text: {{c1::Pumice}} is available in fine/medium/coarse grit and is not suitable for most restorations.
{{c1::Tin oxide}} is a white powder used for polishing teeth and metallic restorations.
{{c1::Sodium bicarbonate}} is the most common air-polishing powder; it removes heavy stains from enamel.
Sodium bicarbonate air polishing is NOT safe for {{c1::composites}}, {{c2::cements}}, or {{c3::exposed roots}}.
{{c1::Aluminum trihydroxide}} is the sodium-free air-polishing powder for enamel, used in {{c2::salt-restricted}} patients; it is not safe for esthetic restorations.
{{c1::Glycine}} air-polishing powder is very gentle; safe for subgingival use, root surfaces and implants; used in periodontal maintenance care.
{{c1::Erythritol}} has the smallest particle size — even gentler than glycine; ideal for biofilm control in deep pockets and around implants.
{{c1::Calcium carbonate}} is moderately abrasive, found in some prophy pastes and air-polishing powders; used for stain removal when mild grit is preferred.
Sealants are {{c1::physical barriers}} (resin) that prevent bacteria from collecting in the {{c2::pits and fissures}} of occlusal, facial and lingual surfaces.
Deep occlusal pits and fissures are most prevalent on the {{c1::first and second permanent molars}}; seal them soon after {{c2::eruption}}.
{{c1::Primary}} teeth are less retentive for sealants than permanent teeth.
Sealants are contraindicated for {{c1::open occlusal lesions}} or {{c2::caries on proximal surfaces}}.
Sealants are {{c1::resin}}-based materials; some sealant materials provide {{c2::fluoride}}.
Sealant retention is {{c1::mechanical}}, through the pores created by the etching process.
{{c1::Saliva contamination}} is the most common reason for sealant failure.
Sealants can be {{c1::self-cured}} or {{c2::light-cured}}.
When etching for a sealant, apply phosphoric acid until the area looks {{c1::chalky and white}}.
After sealant placement check high spots with {{c1::articulating paper}}, the interproximal space by {{c2::flossing the contact}}, and retention with an {{c3::explorer}}.
Most traditional sealants are {{c1::hydrophobic}} and fail with even a tiny bit of saliva; {{c2::moisture-tolerant}} sealants are useful for children and third molars.
Topical fluoride strengthens enamel through {{c1::remineralization}}, inhibits {{c2::acid production}} by plaque bacteria, and slows and reverses early decay.
{{c1::Acidulated phosphate fluoride (APF)}} should not be used on composites, porcelain or glass ionomer restorations — it can {{c2::etch or dull}} the surface.
cloze.extra: Applies to APF foam/gel in trays too.

cloze.text: {{c1::Neutral sodium fluoride (NaF)}} varnish is safe for all surfaces and restorations.
Fluoride toothpaste: apply a {{c1::smear}} for children under 3 and a {{c2::pea-size}} amount for ages 3–6.
cloze.extra: High-fluoride prescription pastes are available for high-risk patients.

cloze.text: Fluoride rinse (daily or weekly) is not recommended for children under {{c1::6}} due to the risk of {{c2::swallowing}}.
After professionally applied fluoride varnish, the patient avoids brushing and eating hard foods for {{c1::4–6 hours}}.
cloze.extra: Varnish is highly concentrated; ideal for children, elderly and high-risk patients.

cloze.text: In-office fluoride foam or gel is applied in {{c1::trays}}.
Nano-hydroxyapatite (n-HAp) is a synthetic form of {{c1::hydroxyapatite}}, the main mineral in enamel and dentin.
n-HAp is used in toothpastes to promote {{c1::enamel remineralization}} and reduce {{c2::dentinal hypersensitivity}}.
A 2021 systematic review found toothpastes with {{c1::10%}} n-HAp had remineralization effects comparable to {{c2::1,000 ppm}} fluoride (OTC dose) in early carious lesions.
cloze.extra: Catch: most commercial n-HAp products contain only 1–5%.

cloze.text: n-HAp particles are small enough to enter {{c1::enamel micro-defects}} and help rebuild lost minerals.
n-HAp is often used as a {{c1::fluoride alternative}} or complement in caries prevention.
n-HAp does not stain, is {{c1::non-toxic}}, and is well tolerated by all ages.
n-HAp is popular in {{c1::Japan}} and Europe and is now found in more OTC products worldwide.
SDF contains {{c1::silver}}, which kills bacteria, and {{c2::fluoride}}, which strengthens tooth structure.
SDF is used to {{c1::arrest active dental caries}} in children, elderly patients, or those who can't tolerate restorative treatment.
SDF is applied topically, especially to {{c1::cavitated lesions without pulp exposure}}.
Advantages of SDF: {{c1::non-invasive and painless}}, fast and inexpensive.
Main drawback of SDF: it {{c1::permanently stains the carious lesion black}} — an esthetic concern, especially on anterior teeth.
SDF does NOT permanently stain {{c1::healthy enamel}} or soft tissue.
Some products include {{c1::potassium iodide (KI)}}, applied after SDF to reduce staining.
In endodontic therapy the pulp is removed, cleaned, then filled with {{c1::gutta-percha}}, which has a {{c2::white/pink}} appearance.
Use a {{c1::rubber dam}} for isolation during endodontic therapy (also useful when placing restorations).
A rubber dam should NOT be used for patients with severe {{c1::breathing}} problems, {{c2::psychological}} problems, and/or {{c3::partially erupted teeth}} (the clamp will not fit).
A periodontal dressing (periodontal {{c1::pack}}) is a bandage that provides comfort, maintains {{c2::blood clotting}}, inhibits {{c3::food impaction}}, and protects the wound.
The periodontal dressing itself does NOT have any {{c1::wound-healing}} properties.
Some periodontal dressings contain {{c1::eugenol}} for its obtundent (soothing) effect, but it may irritate the tissue.
A periodontal dressing must not be higher than the {{c1::height of contour}} or near the occlusal surface; smooth it while still soft.
Push the periodontal dressing into the {{c1::interdental areas}} for better retention; it should harden within hours.
After dressing removal, use {{c1::Charter's}} method of toothbrushing (bristles directed toward the occlusal surface, not the gingiva) if needed.
A bone graft may be indicated to correct bony {{c1::defects}} and for the placement of {{c2::implants}}.
A dental implant is an artificial {{c1::tooth root}} placed into the jaw to hold a replacement tooth or bridge.
cloze.extra: An option for people who lost teeth to periodontal disease, injury or another reason.

cloze.text: {{c1::Endosteal}} implants — screws, cylinders or blades surgically placed into the jawbone — are the {{c2::most commonly used}} type; the screw works as the root.

{{c1::Subperiosteal}} implants sit on top of the jaw with a metal framework whose posts protrude through the gum; used for patients who cannot wear conventional dentures and have {{c2::minimal bone height}}.
{{c1::Transosteal}} implants: a metal plate and posts placed through the entire mandible, from under the chin into the mouth; used only in the {{c2::lower jaw}} and rarely today.
External tooth whitening (bleaching) can lighten {{c1::extrinsic}} stains.
{{c1::Internal}} whitening is done by placing the agent inside an endodontically treated tooth.
{{c1::Yellow}} teeth have better whitening results than {{c2::gray}} teeth.
In-office whitening uses {{c1::30–40%}} hydrogen peroxide.
In-office whitening gel is placed on the enamel about {{c1::2 mm}} thick; gingival tissues are protected with {{c2::petroleum jelly}} or other protective substances.
In-office whitening lights enhance hydrogen peroxide by {{c1::speeding up the chemical reaction}}; common sources are LED, halogen, plasma arc, or laser.
In-home whitening uses {{c1::10–22%}} carbamide peroxide, which equals about {{c2::3–7%}} hydrogen peroxide.
Carbamide peroxide breaks down into {{c1::hydrogen peroxide}} and {{c2::urea}}.
For in-home whitening, trays are {{c1::fabricated in office}} and loaded at home.
Whitening strips contain about {{c1::5%}} hydrogen peroxide (OTC) or up to {{c2::14%}} for professional versions.
In-home whitening works over longer periods, e.g. {{c1::overnight}} or 1–2 hours daily.
Desensitizing toothpaste is recommended {{c1::before and after}} whitening procedures.
Active ingredients of desensitizing toothpaste: {{c1::potassium nitrate}}, sodium citrate, and {{c2::strontium chloride}}.
{{c1::Fluoride varnishes}} are also effective desensitizers.
{{c1::Metals}} (amalgam, gold, PFM, endodontic posts, retention pins) appear radiopaque.
Cements, liners, bases, sealants and gutta-percha appear {{c1::partially (slightly) radiopaque}}.
{{c1::Porcelain}} has a radiopacity similar to enamel.
A PFM crown shows a solid radiopaque {{c1::metal}} center and a slightly less radiopaque {{c2::porcelain}} lining.
Composites vary radiographically: earlier composites lacked metals, but newer composites add {{c1::barium}} and {{c2::strontium}}, so they appear more radiopaque.
Amalgam is completely radiopaque because X-rays {{c1::cannot penetrate metal}}.
Gold is completely radiopaque, whether in a {{c1::crown, inlay, or onlay}}.
Retention pins, posts and pivots appear radiopaque; they {{c1::stabilize and retain}} the restoration and crown in place.
On a radiograph, base material is {{c1::slightly radiopaque}}; it is used to protect the pulp.
On a radiograph, gutta-percha is {{c1::slightly radiopaque}}; it fills the tooth canals.
{{c1::Silver points}} are obsolete metal endodontic filling materials that appear radiopaque; they were replaced due to {{c2::corrosion}} and poor sealing.
Composite is radiopaque, but its opacity density varies with the material's {{c1::composition}}.
Orthodontic appliances appear {{c1::radiopaque}} on radiographs.
Implants appear radiopaque and resemble a {{c1::screw}}; {{c2::metal}} implants are more radiopaque than {{c3::ceramic}} ones.

basic.back: Resin flows into the microscopic pores created by etching and bonds mechanically to the tooth surface

basic.front: After etching, why rinse thoroughly but keep dentin slightly moist?
basic.back: To prevent collapse of the collagen network in the dentin.
Loss of tooth structure by mechanical forces (e.g., caused by polishing)

basic.front: Saliva contaminates the etched enamel during sealant placement. What do you do?
basic.back: Re-etch the tooth for a shorter amount of time.

basic.front: Why do teeth tend to be brittle after endodontic therapy?
basic.back: Loss of blood supply to the tooth.
Bone graft from the patient's own body
Bone graft from the same species, usually cadavers
basic.extra: WakeUpMemory: Greek allos = other — from another human.

basic.back: Bone graft from a different species, usually cows (bovine)

basic.front: Why can whitening cause temporary dentinal hypersensitivity?
basic.back: Peroxide passes through the enamel into the dentin; through the dentinal tubules it reaches and irritates the nerve inside the tooth (a quick, sharp zing).

typein.question: A liner is applied as a thin coating on the surface of the cavity preparation. Usual thickness? (mm)
typein.extra: Liners are thin; bases are thicker and substitute for dentin.

typein.question: Zinc phosphate hardens within how many minutes? (number)
Polycarboxylate cement should be applied within how many minutes of mixing? (number)
Etchant is commonly what percentage phosphoric acid? (%)
Polishing a restoration is usually performed how many hours after placement? (number)
Polishing with medium-grit paste can remove up to how many microns of enamel in 30 seconds? (number)
typein.extra: Small compared with total enamel thickness, but repeated polishing causes unnecessary wear — hence selective polishing.

typein.question: A periodontal dressing is removed after how many days? (range)

mcq.question: A deep preparation will be restored with composite. Which liner/base material should be AVOIDED under it?
mcq.explanation: Eugenol in ZOE interferes with polymerization and prevents resin from setting. Polycarboxylate is specifically noted as useful under composites because it does not interfere with polymerization.

mcq.question: Which cement produces an exothermic setting reaction, so it is mixed on a cool glass slab?
mcq.explanation: Zinc phosphate (zinc oxide + phosphoric acid) releases heat on mixing; the cool slab dissipates it. Polycarboxylate's reaction does NOT release heat.

mcq.question: A patient on a physician-ordered sodium-restricted diet has heavy extrinsic stain on natural enamel. Which air-polishing powder is most appropriate?
mcq.explanation: Aluminum trihydroxide is the sodium-free alternative for enamel stain in salt-restricted patients. Sodium bicarbonate removes heavy stain but contains sodium; glycine and erythritol are low-abrasion biofilm powders, not heavy-stain powders.

mcq.question: Which practice minimizes loss of tooth structure during polishing?
options: A. Using a coarse, hard grit at high speed
B. Polishing every tooth at every visit
C. Selective polishing with lubrication and light pressure
D. Increasing pressure to shorten polishing time
mcq.answer: C. Selective polishing with lubrication and light pressure
mcq.explanation: Selective polishing preserves tooth structure; lubrication prevents overheating. Larger/harder grit, more pressure and more speed all increase abrasion.

mcq.question: A high-caries-risk patient has porcelain crowns and composite restorations. Which professional fluoride is the best choice?
mcq.explanation: Neutral NaF varnish is safe for all surfaces and restorations. APF (gel or foam) is acidic and can etch or dull porcelain, composites and glass ionomer.

mcq.question: A frail nursing-home resident has several cavitated root-caries lesions without pulp exposure and cannot tolerate restorative treatment. Which material is most appropriate to arrest the lesions?
mcq.explanation: SDF arrests active caries in cavitated lesions without pulp exposure and suits patients who can't tolerate restorations. n-HAp remineralizes micro-defects but does not arrest cavitated lesions; sealants are contraindicated over open lesions.

mcq.question: Which statement about periodontal dressings is correct?
options: A. The dressing promotes wound healing
B. It should extend onto the occlusal surface for retention
C. It is pushed into the interdental areas for retention
D. It is removed after 24 hours
mcq.answer: C. It is pushed into the interdental areas for retention
mcq.explanation: Pushing the soft dressing interdentally gives retention. The dressing has no wound-healing properties, must stay below the height of contour, and is removed after 5–7 days.

mcq.question: An edentulous patient cannot wear conventional dentures and has minimal mandibular bone height. Which implant type sits on top of the bone under the periosteum to support a prosthesis?
mcq.explanation: Subperiosteal implants rest on the jaw with posts through the gum — for minimal bone height. Endosteal implants need enough bone to place a screw into it.

mcq.question: A radiograph of an older root-canal-treated molar shows thin, very radiopaque lines in the canals, and the tooth has periapical failure. What filling material was most likely used?
mcq.explanation: Silver points are obsolete metal canal fillers — fully radiopaque — replaced because of corrosion and poor sealing. Gutta-percha is only slightly radiopaque.

mcq.question: Which cement releases fluoride and chemically bonds to tooth structure?
mcq.explanation: Glass ionomer cements release fluoride and form a chemical bond with enamel and dentin, making them ideal for high-caries-risk patients.

mcq.question: Which type of gypsum product has the highest compressive strength and is used for die fabrication?
options: D. Type IV — High-strength dental stone
mcq.answer: D. Type IV — High-strength dental stone
mcq.explanation: Type IV gypsum has the lowest expansion and highest strength, ideal for precise dies and castings in prosthodontics.

mcq.question: Which dental material has the highest thermal conductivity?
mcq.explanation: Amalgam is a metal and conducts heat very well. This is why a base or liner is often used underneath to protect the pulp.

mcq.question: Etching enamel with phosphoric acid primarily affects the enamel by:
mcq.explanation: Etching enamel with phosphoric acid dissolves hydroxyapatite crystals to create microporosities for micromechanical retention.

mcq.question: A base material used to insulate the pulp should ideally have which properties?
options: A. High solubility and low strength
B. High thermal conductivity and low elasticity
C. Low thermal conductivity and adequate compressive strength
D. Low film thickness and acidic pH
mcq.answer: C. Low thermal conductivity and adequate compressive strength
mcq.explanation: Bases protect the pulp from temperature changes and mechanical forces, so they must insulate well and have decent strength.

mcq.question: Which component in amalgam increases strength and corrosion resistance?
mcq.explanation: High-copper amalgams improve strength and corrosion resistance.

mcq.question: What property allows a dental material to return to its original shape after deformation?
mcq.explanation: Elasticity is the ability of a material to return to its original shape after a deforming force is removed — important in impression materials and orthodontic wires.

mcq.question: Which liner is known for its sedative effect on the pulp?
mcq.explanation: Eugenol has a soothing, sedative effect on the pulp, which is why ZOE is used as a liner or temporary cement in deep cavities.

mcq.question: Which is true of hybrid composites?
options: A. They contain only large filler particles
B. They polish better than microfills
C. They offer a balance of strength and esthetics
D. They are used only for posterior restorations
mcq.answer: C. They offer a balance of strength and esthetics
mcq.explanation: Hybrid composites contain both large and small filler particles, providing good strength and decent polishability for both anterior and posterior use.

mcq.question: Why is nano-hydroxyapatite especially useful in managing sensitivity?
options: C. It fills enamel micro-defects and seals dentinal tubules
mcq.answer: C. It fills enamel micro-defects and seals dentinal tubules
mcq.explanation: It fills micro-defects in enamel and seals open dentinal tubules, helping reduce sensitivity by blocking fluid movement.

mcq.question: Which is the most critical factor affecting the long-term success of a pit and fissure sealant?
options: A. Using a fluoride-containing sealant material
B. Allowing the etchant to remain on enamel for at least 10 seconds
C. Achieving a strong chemical bond to the enamel surface
D. Preventing contamination of the etched enamel prior to sealant application
mcq.answer: D. Preventing contamination of the etched enamel prior to sealant application
mcq.explanation: After etching, the enamel surface becomes porous to allow micromechanical retention. If saliva or moisture contaminates the surface, it disrupts this bonding and greatly increases the chance of sealant failure. Chemical bonding is not the main mechanism here; it's mechanical retention.

mcq.question: Which of the following is true about applying SDF on anterior teeth?
options: A. It should be avoided unless aesthetics are not a concern
B. It removes intrinsic stains during application
C. It bonds better to enamel than to dentin
D. It reverses existing white spot lesions
mcq.answer: A. It should be avoided unless aesthetics are not a concern
mcq.explanation: SDF stains decayed areas black. On front teeth this is very visible, so it's avoided unless esthetics don't matter.

mcq.question: Which air polishing powder is safest to use around implants and exposed root surfaces?
mcq.explanation: Glycine is a very low-abrasion powder that's safe for subgingival use and on delicate surfaces like roots and implants.

mcq.question: On a radiograph, which material appears most radiopaque?
mcq.explanation: Amalgam is a metal-based material and appears bright white (radiopaque) on X-rays.

mcq.question: What causes composite to fail more often over time compared to amalgam?
options: B. Higher thermal expansion and shrinkage
mcq.answer: B. Higher thermal expansion and shrinkage
mcq.explanation: Composite expands and contracts more than tooth structure, increasing the risk of microleakage and restoration failure over time.
